etymologies.etymologyHTML: Borrowed from Latin continens, noun use of present participle of continēre (“to contain”).

definitions.definition: One of the main continuous landmasses, separated by water or geological features, on the surface of a planet, sometimes including its continental shelves and the islands on them.

quote.citation: 1850, [Alfred, Lord Tennyson], In Memoriam, London: Edward Moxon, […], →OCLC, Canto XXXV, page 54:
quote.text: But I should turn mine ears and hearThe moanings of the homeless sea,⁠The sound of streams that swift or slow⁠Draw down Æonian hills, and sowThe dust of continents to be;  […]

definitions.definition: Each of the traditional main regions into which the Earth’s land surface is divided, including both an extent of mainland and various conventionally associated islands, etc; namely, Africa, Europe, Asia, Australasia/Oceania, North America, South America, and Antarctica.

(obsolete in general sense) A large contiguous landmass as opposed to its islands, peninsulas, and so forth; mainland. Also specifically, the Old World continent of Europe–Asia–Africa: see the Continent.

quote.citation: 1624, John Donne, “17. Meditation”, in Deuotions upon Emergent Occasions, and Seuerall Steps in My Sicknes: […], London:  […]  A[ugustine] M[atthews] for Thomas Iones, →OCLC, pages 415–416:
quote.text: No man is an Iland, intire of it ſelfe; euery man is a peece of the Continent, a part of the maine;  […]

definitions.definition: (figurative) A large connected expanse of something in general.
(obsolete) Any continuous tract or area of land; country, connected region.
(obsolete) Land (as opposed to the water), dry land.

quote.citation: 1590, Edmund Spenser, “Book III, Canto V”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC:
quote.text: The carkas with the streame was carried downe, / But th’head fell backeward on the continent.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) The body or mass of a celestial body such as the sun or moon.
(obsolete) Container, vessel, something that holds or contains something else.
(obsolete) The principal or essential points of something viewed collectively: sum, summary, substance.

quote.citation: c. 1596–1598 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Merchant of Venice”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene ii]:
quote.text: […]  Here's the scroll,The continent and summary of my fortune.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English contynent, from Old French continent, from Latin continentem (“continuous; holding together”), present participle of continēre (“to contain”).

definitions.definition: Exercising self-restraint; controlled, temperate with respect to one’s bodily needs or passions, especially sex.

quote.citation: c. 1603–1604 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Othello, the Moore of Venice”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene i]:
quote.text: Have a continent forbearance till the speed of his rage goes slower.

quote.citation: 1926, T.E. Lawrence, Seven Pillars of Wisdom, New York: Anchor, published 1991, page 219:
quote.text: Their strength was the strength of men geographically beyond temptation: the poverty of Arabia made them simple, continent, enduring.

quote.citation: 2009, Diarmaid MacCulloch, A History of Christianity, Penguin, published 2010, page 119:
quote.text: A celibate himself, he was of the opinion that marriage was something of a concession to human frailty, to save from fornication those who could not be continent, so it was better to marry than to burn with lust.

definitions.definition: Having voluntary control over one’s urination or defecation.
(obsolete) Not interrupted; connected; continuous, whether in time or space.

quote.citation: c. 1587–1588, [Christopher Marlowe], Tamburlaine the Great.  […]  The First Part […], 2nd edition, part 1, London:  […]  [R. Robinson for] Richard Iones, […], published 1592, →OCLC; reprinted as Tamburlaine the Great (A Scolar Press Facsimile), Menston, Yorkshire, London: Scolar Press, 1973, →ISBN, Act I, scene i:
quote.text: Affrike and Europe bordering on your land,And continent to your Dominions:  […]

quote.citation: 1843, John McIntosh, The Origin of the North American Indians:
quote.text: The northeast part of Asia is, if not continent with the west side of America, yet certainly it is the least disjoined by sea of all that coast.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) Serving to restrain or limit; restraining; opposing.

quote.citation: c. 1595–1596 (date written), W. Shakespere [i.e., William Shakespeare], A Pleasant Conceited Comedie Called, Loues Labors Lost. […] (First Quarto), London:  […]  W[illiam] W[hite] for Cut[h]bert Burby, published 1598, →OCLC; republished as Shakspere’s Loves Labours Lost (Shakspere-Quarto Facsimiles; no. 5), London: W[illiam] Griggs, […], [1880], →OCLC, [Act I, scene i]:
quote.text: There did I ſee that low ſpirited Swaine, [...] hight Coſtard, (Clow[ne]. O mee) ſorted and conſorted contrary to thy eſtabliſhed proclaymed Edict and continent Cannon; Which with, o with, but with this I paſſion to ſay wherewith: / Clo[wne]. With a Wench.

quote.citation: c. 1599–1602 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Hamlet, Prince of Denmarke”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene iv]:
quote.text: Have a continent forbearance till the speed of his rage goes slower.
